cards.a: Classification, marking, policy maps, and interface counters. Failures show as no marking, wrong queueing, or drops despite a policy.

cards.q: What command shows the applied state and counters of a QoS policy?
cards.a: show policy-map interface, which shows the applied policy and its counters.
Classify, mark, police/shape, queue, then monitor. Class to mark to enforce to queue to observe.

cards.q: What are the top QoS traps?
cards.a: Direction (service-policy in/out) and the trust boundary, which determines whether markings are preserved.

cards.q: How does the trust boundary differ between L2 and L3?
cards.a: Trust COS is used on switches (Layer 2) and trust DSCP on routers (Layer 3). An untrusted port remarks markings.

cards.q: What does a zero counter on a class indicate?
cards.a: The class never matched any traffic, so the classification or the applied direction is wrong.

cards.q: Queue drops behind a policy do not always mean what?
cards.a: They do not always indicate policy failure, but rather congestion. Drops behind a policy point to queueing/congestion.

cards.q: What command shows the trust configuration on a switch?
How do you apply a QoS policy to an interface?
cards.a: With the service-policy output QOS command (direction matters: service-policy in or out) under the interface.

cards.q: What do class-map and policy-map commands do?
cards.a: A class-map defines match rules (classification); a policy-map applies actions like priority or bandwidth to the matched classes.

cards.q: What QoS mechanisms handle congestion-induced drops?
cards.a: Shaping and WRED. WRED drops packets under congestion, and shaping smooths traffic.

cards.q: Priority percent 10 and bandwidth percent 20 in a policy represent what?
cards.a: A priority (strict/low-latency) queue of 10% and a bandwidth guarantee of 20% for the respective classes.
